subject: economics
title: The Short-Run Phillips Curve
welcome_lead: A trade-off between unemployment and inflation - in the short run.
meta_desc: A-Level Phillips Curve: original short-run trade-off.
final_note: Short-run trade-off works only when expectations are stuck.

concepts.def: 1958 - UK data showed a stable inverse relationship.
Period before wage and price expectations adjust.

Wages slow to adjust to inflation expectations.

walkthroughs.body_html: A.W. Phillips analysed UK wage and unemployment data from 1861 to 1957 and found an inverse relationship - high inflation went with low unemployment.
When AD rises, firms hire more workers (cutting unemployment) and raise prices (creating inflation). With sticky wages, real wages fall and labour demand jumps.
1960s policymakers tried to pick a point on the curve - accepting more inflation to push unemployment down. The 1970s would show this strategy collapsing.

options: Inflation against GDP
Inflation against unemployment
Unemployment against wages only
Investment against savings

mcqs.q: What did the original Phillips curve suggest, and how has thinking changed?
options: Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
The Phillips curve still proves you can always reduce unemployment by allowing more inflation.
The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.

The original Phillips curve suggested a stable inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Friedman and the 1970s stagflation experience added expectations — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
Inflation is when prices are high.
A sustained rise in the general price level over time — reducing the purchasing power of money. Measured by the percentage change in a price index.
The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.

mcqs.q: How does raising interest rates reduce inflation?
options: Higher interest rates make money more valuable so inflation falls automatically.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reducing consumption and investment — lowering aggregate demand and slowing price rises.
Higher interest rates directly force shops to lower their prices.
